title: Delhi High Court Upholds Nil Arbitral Award for NHAI, Says Extra-Work Claims Need Proof
meta_description: Delhi High Court dismisses a contractor's Section 34 challenge to a nil award, holding extra-work claims on an NHAI highway contract need actual proof.
case_name: Abhoy Charan Bakshi v. National Highways Authority of India & Anr.
body: A contractor who repairs rain-damaged road stretches without first getting the authority's sign-off on the extra work takes on the risk of never being paid for it, however genuine the repairs turn out to be. The Delhi High Court made that point in dismissing a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, brought by a highway maintenance contractor against a nil arbitral award that had rejected his claims against the National Highways Authority of India in full.

The dispute traced back to a short-term maintenance contract NHAI awarded to Abhoy Charan Bakshi around December 2005, worth about Rs. 4.37 crore, covering the Baharampore to Farakka stretch of National Highway 34 in West Bengal. Bakshi's claim centred on repair work he said he had carried out after rain damage to the carriageway, work NHAI never agreed to pay for separately. NHAI, on its side, encashed a performance bank guarantee of Rs. 43.74 lakh and withheld a security deposit of Rs. 35.27 lakh, treating the defects as the contractor's own failure to maintain the stretch rather than an event entitling him to extra payment.

The arbitral tribunal split on the outcome. Its majority rejected every one of Bakshi's claims in an award dated November 30, 2022, effectively a nil award in the contractor's favour, while one member took the view that at least partial relief was warranted. Bakshi challenged the majority view before the Delhi High Court, arguing that the tribunal had failed to properly account for the rain damage and the repairs he said followed from it.

Justice Subramonium Prasad was not persuaded. The judgment rests on two distinct propositions that regularly come up together in Section 34 petitions over construction and maintenance contracts. First, a contractor claiming payment for work beyond the scope of the written agreement has to show, with evidence the tribunal can actually weigh, that the work was carried out and what it cost, not merely assert that rain damage occurred and repairs followed. Second, and this is the narrower procedural point that did the real work in disposing of the petition, a court exercising Section 34 jurisdiction does not re-weigh the evidence that was before the arbitrators or substitute its own appreciation of the facts for a plausible view the tribunal has already taken. Where the majority view is one a reasonable tribunal could reach on the record before it, the court will not step into the arbitrators' shoes merely because a dissenting member took a different line.

That combination left Bakshi with little room to manoeuvre. He was not simply asking the court to correct a legal error in how the tribunal read the contract. He was asking it to look again at a factual dispute over whether the extra work had happened and been proved to the tribunal's satisfaction, which is exactly the kind of reappreciation that Section 34, as consistently interpreted since the 2015 amendments narrowed the grounds of challenge, does not permit. The performance guarantee encashment and the withheld security deposit stood as a result, since both were premised on the same underlying finding that the contractor had not shown his repair claims to be well founded.

For contractors working under long-term maintenance contracts on national highways, where rain damage, flooding and seasonal wear routinely generate disputes over what counts as ordinary maintenance against what counts as separately billable extra work, the ruling is a reminder that contemporaneous documentation decides these cases long before any arbitration begins. A claim built after the fact, however plausible the underlying facts may sound, runs into the same wall that stopped Bakshi: a tribunal that is not shown the proof is entitled to reject the claim, and a court reviewing that rejection under Section 34 is not going to go looking for the proof itself.

The ruling also reinforces how narrow the Delhi High Court is prepared to read its own supervisory role over infrastructure arbitrations generally, at a time when NHAI and other highway authorities face a steady stream of Section 34 petitions from contractors on terminated or disputed contracts. A nil award against a contractor is not, on this reasoning, something a reviewing court will disturb simply because a different arbitrator, or a different judge, might have weighed the same facts differently.
why_it_matters: Highway maintenance and EPC contractors routinely face disputes with NHAI over whether repair work beyond the contracted scope is separately payable, especially after monsoon damage. This ruling confirms that Section 34 courts will not reappreciate the factual record to rescue a claim the arbitral tribunal found unproved, which makes contemporaneous proof of extra work, not after-the-fact assertion, the decisive factor in whether such claims survive arbitration and subsequent court challenge.
card_summary: Delhi High Court dismisses a contractor's challenge to a nil arbitral award, holding NHAI's encashment of his performance guarantee stands where his extra-work claims were never proved to the tribunal.
card_tip: Document extra work on a highway contract with photographs and timely notice to the authority before the work is done, since a Section 34 court will not reweigh unproved claims for you.
verification_notes: The case name, citation (O.M.P. (COMM) 107/2023), bench (Justice Subramonium Prasad), decision date (October 13, 2026), contract value (about Rs. 4.37 crore), the stretch covered (Baharampore-Farakka, NH-34, West Bengal), the nil majority award dated November 30, 2022, and the court's reasoning on Section 34's limited scope are corroborated across LiveLawBiz's report and the Indian Kanoon case listing, which independently records the same decision date. One source's figure for the performance bank guarantee (Rs. 43.74 lakh) and security deposit (Rs. 35.27 lakh) is used as reported by LiveLawBiz; other secondary blog summaries gave conflicting figures for the total amount Bakshi had originally claimed (ranging from about Rs. 5.51 crore to about Rs. 20 crore across different write-ups), so that disputed total is left out of this report rather than stated as fact.
